title: Razor Vault
summary: A centralized privacy gateway proposed for Razorpay — moving from static role-based permissions to intent-based access control, built for the DPDP Act 2023 enforcement deadline and India's largest fintech IPO moment.

sections.heading: The Opportunity
sections.body: Razorpay isn't just a payment gateway — it is the infrastructure layer beneath 12 million merchants, from D2C brands to India's largest unicorns. Every checkout, every UPI transfer, every loan disbursed through Razorpay Capital leaves behind a trail of sensitive personal data. At this scale, data isn't a byproduct. It is the product. And the DPDP Act 2023 changes the rules — full penalty enforcement begins May 2027. That window is closing fast.

sections.heading: The Regulatory Catalyst
sections.body: India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act received Presidential assent on August 11, 2023 — the first comprehensive data protection law in India with real teeth. The Rules were notified on November 13, 2025. Full penalty enforcement begins May 13, 2027. Every month of delay is engineering capacity lost. The companies that treat DPDP as a legal checkbox will spend money and generate zero return. Razorpay can do something different.

items.heading: DPDP Act receives Presidential assent
items.body: Legal framework established. Data fiduciaries formally put on notice. India joins the global data protection order alongside GDPR and CCPA.

items.heading: DPDP Rules 2025 notified by MeitY
items.body: Consent, breach notification timelines, Significant Data Fiduciary (SDF) obligations, and the Data Protection Board constitution — now operational.

items.heading: The compliance build window — today
items.body: Companies have a shrinking runway to implement 'reasonable security safeguards.' Every month of delay is a month of engineering time lost before the hard deadline.

items.heading: Full penalty enforcement begins
items.body: Monetary sanctions become enforceable. Non-compliance at this point is no longer a risk — it's a certainty of loss. Up to ₹500 Cr in combined penalties per incident.

sections.heading: The Core Problem
sections.body: The danger isn't always an external hacker. At Razorpay's scale of ~4,000 employees, the highest-risk access points are internal. Every support agent who opens a customer record, every analyst running a SQL query, every engineer debugging a failed transaction — each is a potential exposure event. Not because they're malicious. Because the system gives them far more than they need, by default. This is the structural failure of static Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): it governs access at the door, not at the field.

sections.text: Role sprawl, static permissions in dynamic environments, and outdated roles that no longer reflect real-world responsibilities can all dilute RBAC's effectiveness. The solution is not better role hygiene — it is a more expressive access control model.

sections.heading: The Solution — Razor Vault
sections.body: Razor Vault is a centralized privacy gateway for Razorpay's internal data infrastructure. It moves the company from static role-based permissions — where access is determined once, at role assignment — to intent-based access control, where every request for sensitive data must declare a purpose, is evaluated in real time against a policy engine, and returns only the minimum data required for that stated intent. A support agent, a data analyst, and an on-call engineer can all 'access customer data' — but never see the same data twice, because what they receive is shaped by what they declared they needed it for.

items.title: Format-Preserving Encryption
items.desc: PII encrypted at rest in a format that preserves operational utility. No system rewrites required — the data layer changes, everything on top stays the same.

items.title: Dynamic Field-Level Masking
items.desc: Access-time rendering of only the fields required for the declared intent. Same database, entirely different view per role and per stated purpose.

items.title: Blind Indexing
items.desc: Search functionality preserved without exposing raw PII. HMAC-based — the index carries no readable data but enables exact-match lookups.

sections.label: The Strategic Insight
sections.body: The compliance moat is not a cost center — it's a sales motion. A verifiable, auditable privacy layer becomes the answer to every enterprise procurement questionnaire that currently blocks Razorpay from BFSI and healthcare accounts. Stripe and Adyen didn't build GDPR compliance to avoid fines. They built it to sell to European banks and hospitals. India's DPDP Act creates the identical unlock — but only for whoever moves first.

sections.heading: How It Works — User Experience
sections.body: When a support agent opens a dispute ticket, they declare intent: 'Resolve billing dispute.' The policy engine evaluates: this intent requires last 4 digits of payment method, transaction amount, and merchant name. The agent sees exactly those fields — nothing more. When the same agent escalates to an engineer for a technical investigation, the engineer declares: 'Debug payment failure.' The same customer record now shows a different set of fields shaped by a different intent. The database hasn't changed. The trust surface just became infinitely smaller.

items.title: Data taxonomy & sensitivity classification
items.desc: Map every PII field across Razorpay's systems into tiers: Critical (bank account, PAN), Sensitive (phone, email), Internal (transaction metadata). This becomes the vault's schema.

items.title: Policy engine design
items.desc: Define intent-to-field mappings: each valid business intent (dispute resolution, fraud investigation, merchant onboarding) maps to a specific field allowlist. Zero fields outside the allowlist are returned.

items.title: Format-preserving encryption layer
items.desc: Wrap the existing data store with FPE. Bank account 9876543210 becomes 4829103847 — same format, different value, fully reversible only by the vault service. No app rewrites.

items.title: Audit trail & break-glass protocol
items.desc: Every data access is logged with: who, what intent, what fields returned, timestamp. Break-glass emergency access exists but creates an immutable audit event reviewable by compliance.

items.title: Enterprise compliance API surface
items.desc: Expose a compliance API that generates instant audit reports for enterprise merchant procurement teams, regulators, and the Data Protection Board — turning compliance from internal cost to customer-facing feature.

sections.heading: Business Impact
sections.body: The build cost is estimated at ₹30–50 Cr over 18 months — roughly 1% of Razorpay's FY25 revenue. The risk avoidance is ₹400–500 Cr in potential DPDP penalties. But the real ROI is strategic: every BFSI and healthcare merchant that currently can't onboard a non-compliant payments vendor becomes accessible. That's a new enterprise segment, unlocked by a compliance investment.

sections.label: What I'd do differently
sections.body: I'd start the data taxonomy work earlier, as a standalone zero-cost initiative before any engineering begins. Mapping every PII field and its sensitivity tier across all Razorpay services is the riskiest unknown in this proposal — it could take 2 months or 6 depending on how well internal APIs are documented. Starting there buys optionality on the build timeline.
